transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi... yeah. Um, well, I'm here because of these lesson videos I have to record for my classes. Ever since the school district switched to this new portal system, the video software is just... well, actually, the IT guy, Dave, he never responds to my tickets anyway. He's always supposedly "busy" setting up the projectors in the auditorium, which they haven't even used since the spring play. 

But anyway, I have to look at these lesson videos, and... I just can't stop seeing it. The side of my face, it's just so crooked and swollen-looking. It's completely awful. And once I notice it... I mean, Tyler in my third period is always squinting at the screen, though he claims he just needs glasses. Kids these days have terrible eyesight from their phones, and their posture is totally ruined too. I tell them to sit up, but they don't care. 

But I just know... I feel like all of them, the students, the parents who watch over their shoulders, the other staff... they must just be staring at that swollen side of my face instead of actually listening to a single word I'm saying.
Do you find yourself spending a lot of time thinking about the way your face looks, and does it cause you a lot of distress or interfere with your daily life?

Yeah, I mean... it's all I think about. It's totally ruining everything. I've fallen so far behind on my lesson planning, which is a nightmare because the new curriculum standards they rolled out this year are incredibly dense. They expect us to integrate all this cross-disciplinary stuff, and the science department head, Karen, is always breathing down our necks about it. She's been there for like twenty years and thinks her way is the only way, but honestly, her biology labs are completely outdated. 

But anyway, yeah, I can't get anything done. I'm supposed to be mentoring the new student teachers, and I'm the assistant coach for the JV basketball team. We actually had a decent shot at making it to regionals this year, we have this kid, Marcus, who has a crazy good three-point shot. But I'm just never there, or I'm there but I'm completely distracted, thinking about my face. I just leave early or skip practice because I can't handle the thought of people looking at me under those horrible gym lights. They're fluorescent, you know? They make everyone look terrible, but for me, it just highlights how crooked everything is. 

So much of my work just never gets finished on time anymore. The administrators have started documenting all my missed deadlines and the times I haven't shown up for coverage. Principal Higgins actually called me into his office last week... his office always smells like stale coffee and those cheap pine air fresheners. But he had this whole folder, just documenting everything. I'm really worried I'm close to losing my position. I just... I can't focus on teaching when my face looks like this.

When you're worried about your face during the videos or in person, is it mainly about the specific way your face looks — like the crookedness or swelling — or is it more about a general fear that others are judging or noticing something wrong with you?

Um, well, it's definitely the swelling and the crookedness. That's the main thing. Like, if my face didn't look so messed up on that one side, I wouldn't even be thinking about what other people are thinking, you know? It's just that it's so obvious. Like, how could they not be staring at it? Especially on those videos. The camera quality is actually pretty good, which is part of the problem. They bought these new webcams for all the classrooms last semester using some grant money. The district actually got a ton of funding for tech upgrades, but of course, they spent half of it on these interactive whiteboards that nobody knows how to use. Mrs. Gable in history refuses to even turn hers on. She just writes on the whiteboard next to it. 

But yeah, the webcams pick up every single detail. So when I'm recording, I know exactly what they're seeing. It's not just a general worry that they don't like me or something. It's specifically that they're looking at my face, at how swollen it is, and thinking, "Wow, what is wrong with him?" And then I just spiral, you know? I can't even get through the lesson on the respiratory system without losing my place. Which is a shame, because I usually have this really great analogy using a balloon and a plastic bottle, but I just... I can't even get through it anymore.
